holding_summary: A householder who lets two rooms of his dwelling to tenants is treated under ordinary landlord-tenant law, and in the absence of fraud or concealment is not liable to the tenant for injuries from a defect existing at the time of the demise. The rule of caveat emptor applies in full force, requiring the tenant to use ordinary care to discover open defects, including those in shared means of ingress/egress.

quotes.text: October 5, 1914, plaintiffs leased two rooms on the third floor of defendant’s house, and had lived in the premises five days when an accident occurred.

In the absence of fraud or concealment a landlord is not responsible for injuries resulting from defects existing at the time of the demise: 16 Ruling Case LaAV, p. 1059; Borggard v. Gale, 205 Ill. 511. The rule of caveat emptor applies in full force and the tenant and his family are bound to use their eyes to discover such defects as are open to observation or inspection: 24 Cyc. 1114.
The rule of caveat emptor applies in full force and the tenant and his family are bound to use their eyes to discover such defects as are open to observation or inspection

notes: Landlord let two rooms of his own house to a tenant family sharing a common drying platform with other occupants; court applies ordinary lease/caveat-emptor doctrine without special disability, treating the room-letting as an ordinary incident of ownership. Exact lease term not stated (only that plaintiffs had occupied five days at time of accident).

holding_summary: A divorce libellant could not establish legal Pennsylvania residence merely by showing he rented a room in a Philadelphia rooming house for $15 a month and stayed there on average two nights a week, while paying no local taxes, voting nowhere, having no Pennsylvania business, and keeping his family ties in New Jersey. The court treated his occasional, temporary rooming-house stays as legally insufficient to establish a true, fixed, permanent residence.

quotes.text: the husband, who is thirty-eight years of age, rented a room in a rooming house in Philadelphia, in April, 1915, for the sum of $15 a month, which was later reduced to $12.

A libellant in divorce cannot establish the fact of a legal residence in Pennsylvania, by proof that he rented a room in a rooming house in Philadelphia for the sum of fifteen dollars a month, that he spent on an average at least two nights a week at the house during the year
His irregular occasional and temporary stay in the Philadelphia boarding house shows the lack of all the essential elements in establishing a true, fixed, permanent residence.

notes: Not a case adjudicating the legality of room-letting itself; it uses the paid rooming-house stay as evidence that occupant lacked a bona fide domicile. Included because the court squarely characterizes the legal nature of a paid rooming-house stay (transient, not residence) — polarity marked mixed as it neither validates nor restricts the letting practice, but treats lodger occupancy as legally lesser than tenancy/domicile.
